title: Eiffel Tower Gender Row Over BAPS Visit Unites French Politicians, Splits Diaspora
excerpt: A private BAPS visit to the Eiffel Tower that sidelined female staff united French politicians across the spectrum — while splitting the Indian diaspora over accountability and backlash.
body:
• A private September 5 visit by a 100-strong BAPS delegation to the Eiffel Tower led to female staff being moved off their posts, triggering a staff strike that closed the tower on September 7.
  • The tower's operator admitted the delegation had asked to limit "interactions with women" and said those conditions should never have been accepted; politicians from the Socialists to the far right condemned the episode.
  • BAPS says the request was never rooted in gender and apologised for any pain caused, pointing to its record on women's participation.
  • Within the Indian diaspora, the row has split progressives — who warn against anti-Hindu backlash but also against conflating BAPS with Hinduism — from defenders who say the episode is being used to stain India's image.

A private visit to the Eiffel Tower by a delegation of the Hindu organisation BAPS has become a national political row in France, uniting politicians across the spectrum in condemnation — and dividing the Indian diaspora over what the episode means.

On Saturday, September 5, a delegation of about 100 people linked to BAPS — the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha — made a private visit to the tower arranged for the start of normal opening hours. The tower's operator, SETE, acknowledged that the delegation had requested the visit be organised to limit "interactions with women" — and then admitted "these conditions should not have been accepted."

Staff union representatives said that as the delegation passed, female employees were asked to leave their workstations so men could take their places, leaving women feeling humiliated. On Monday, September 7, staff walked out; the tower closed, with signs citing "operational reasons," before reopening on Tuesday, September 8. Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire ordered an investigation, calling the staff's anger "legitimate."

A united political front

The condemnation crossed every political line. Aurore Bergé, the minister for gender equality, called the alleged incident "unacceptable," declaring: "In France, gender equality is neither negotiable nor subject to varying standards. It is a principle, and there are no exceptions to it." Yaël Braun-Pivet, president of the National Assembly, said: "I refuse to accept that women should be told to step aside to meet the demands of foreign visitors." Valérie Pécresse of the centre-right Les Républicains, president of the Île-de-France region, expressed shock — notable because she had presided over the inauguration of BAPS's new temple just a day later. And Marine Le Pen, the far-right presidential candidate, said: "In France, we will never accept that the presence of women be 'limited.'"

"In France, we do not ask women to erase themselves. No dogma, no religion is above the laws of the Republic."

— Aurore Bergé, France's Minister for Gender Equality

BAPS's response

BAPS said the visit was pre-coordinated with the tower's team, adding that "to our knowledge, at no time was access to the Eiffel Tower denied to anyone. Nevertheless, we sincerely apologise for any pain or inconvenience caused." BAPS Paris told CNN: "It was never, at any point, intended as a request rooted in gender, and any suggestion to the contrary does not reflect the spirit or values of our fellowship or the delegation."

Religious scholar Yogi Trivedi noted the sect's Swaminarayan monastic tradition of celibacy and said more than half of the BAPS fellowship is female, with a record of advocating women's rights. Some defenders argued on social media that the episode was being used to stain India's credibility and the Hindu religion.

The temple and the festival

The visit was not a Diwali event. It was part of a 13-day "festival of culture" from September 3 to 14 marking the inauguration of BAPS's first major temple in France, in the Paris suburb of Bussy-Saint-Georges — believed to be Europe's largest traditional-style Hindu temple, inaugurated on September 6 with a video message from Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who said it would "energise the cultural relations between India and France." The festivities included a September 5 boat procession on the Seine with more than 5,500 devotees.

India's Ministry of External Affairs distanced the government from the tower episode. Spokesman Randhir Jaiswal called it "a matter purely between the entities concerned" and described Modi's virtual inauguration message as routine goodwill, unrelated to the controversy.

The diaspora splits

Among Indians in France, the row has exposed a fault line. On the same day as the tower visit, the Indian Alliance Paris — co-hosted with the CGT union — held a public meeting warning about BAPS and the spread of Hindu nationalism, with activists from France, the US and India. IAP secretary Joy Banerjee said the meeting drew little French press coverage: "Suddenly, the mask was dropped on Monday because of the strike." On September 8, the group warned on X that "the Eiffel Tower story must not become fodder for more racism," adding that "BAPS does not represent all Hindus and it certainly does not represent India."

Sunita Viswanath, co-founder of the US-based Hindus for Human Rights, said she was dismayed French authorities had approved the mega-temple given BAPS's controversies in the United States, adding of the tower episode: "It's not a surprise, but it's certainly very disappointing that they weren't paying attention." Nationalist Congress Party spokesperson Anish Gawande called the incident "more than an isolated dispute," warning it could be picked up by far-right narratives about immigrants, religion and national identity.

Background on BAPS

BAPS, founded in 1907 in the Gujarat village of Bochasan, is a denomination of the Swaminarayan Sampradaya, a Vaishnavite sect of Hinduism. It manages more than 1,300 temples and 5,025 centres worldwide, including the BAPS Swaminarayan Akshardham in Robbinsville, New Jersey — the largest Hindu temple in the US — and the UAE's largest Hindu temple, inaugurated by Modi in 2024. It is not unfamiliar with controversy abroad: after a May 2021 FBI raid on its Robbinsville construction site, Indian stone workers sued alleging forced labour and caste-based exploitation; the US Justice Department closed the case in September 2025 without stating a cause.

What's next

The mayor's investigation into the tower visit will determine exactly who agreed to the delegation's conditions and why. For the diaspora, the harder question is already on the table: how to hold a powerful religious institution to account without feeding the racism many fear will follow. As the Indian Alliance Paris put it, the challenge is to keep the story about what happened at the Eiffel Tower — and not let it become about Indians in France.
